```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A mixed model can answer several different questions about the same row of
data. How many visits will a 50-year-old make at clinic C01? At a clinic not
in the data? At a typical clinic? On average across clinics? `ilm_predict()`
makes you name the question, because the answers differ. This vignette works
through the choices: which unit, whether the mean or a new observation, and
how much of the fit's uncertainty to carry, and then the check limn makes when
there are few groups, with its remedy.

```{r setup}
library(limn)
```

## The data and the model

Patients' yearly visits to a clinic depend on their age, and clinics differ.
The simulation below makes data for any number of clinics, 25 patients each,
with the clinics' effects drawn from a normal distribution on the log scale.

```{r data}
simulate_clinics <- function(n_clinics, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  d <- data.frame(clinic = factor(rep(sprintf("C%02d", 1:n_clinics), each = 25)))
  d$age <- round(runif(nrow(d), 20, 80))
  clinic_effect <- rnorm(n_clinics, 0, 0.5)
  d$visits <- rpois(nrow(d), exp(0.3 + 0.02 * (d$age - 50) + clinic_effect[d$clinic]))
  d
}
clinics30 <- simulate_clinics(30, seed = 2026)
fit <- illume::ilm_model(visits ~ I(age - 50) + (1 | clinic), data = clinics30,
                         family = "poisson", verbose = FALSE)
```

## Which unit

The same row, a 50-year-old at clinic C01, predicted four ways:

```{r groups}
row <- data.frame(clinic = "C01", age = 50)
which_unit <- lapply(c("fitted", "new", "typical", "population"), function(g)
  cbind(groups = g, as.data.frame(ilm_predict(fit, row, groups = g, nsim = 1000))))
do.call(rbind, which_unit)
```

These are predictions of the mean number of visits, and each answers a
different question:

* `"fitted"`: clinic C01 itself, with its own estimated effect.
* `"new"`: a clinic not in the data. Its effect is unknown, so it is drawn from
  the fitted distribution of clinics, and the interval is much the widest. Its
  `estimate` is the predictive median, and `mean` the expected value.
* `"typical"`: a clinic whose effect is zero.
* `"population"`: the mean averaged over clinics.

The typical clinic and the population average differ. With a log link, the
mean at the middle clinic is not the average of the clinics' means: here the
average is higher. It agrees, up to simulation error, with the new clinic's
expected value, since a new clinic is a clinic drawn at random. Which of the four to report depends on the
question, so a model with random effects has no default `groups`.

## The mean, or a new observation

`target = "mean"` predicts the expected number of visits. `target = "response"`
predicts one patient's count, which adds the Poisson variation around that
mean:

```{r target}
new_clinic <- data.frame(clinic = "new", age = 50)
rbind(cbind(target = "mean",
            as.data.frame(ilm_predict(fit, new_clinic, target = "mean", groups = "new", nsim = 1000))),
      cbind(target = "response",
            as.data.frame(ilm_predict(fit, new_clinic, target = "response", groups = "new", nsim = 1000))))
```

The mean is the same either way; the interval for one patient is wider, and
in whole visits.

## Averages over a population

A model's predictions can be averaged over a population of rows, draw by draw,
so the average keeps the uncertainty its rows share. `ilm_average()` does this.
Averaged over this sample's own patients, each at their own clinic, the model
gives:

```{r standardise}
p_all <- ilm_predict(fit, clinics30, groups = "fitted", nsim = 500)
as.data.frame(ilm_average(p_all))
```

With population counts as weights, the same average is post-stratification.
Gelman and Hill (2007, section 14.1, equation (14.1)) weight each cell's
prediction by its count in the population. Here the cells are three ages,
averaged over clinics, in a population with more young patients than the
sample:

```{r poststratify}
cells <- data.frame(age = c(30, 50, 70), count = c(500, 300, 200))
p_cells <- ilm_predict(fit, cells, groups = "population", nsim = 500)
as.data.frame(p_cells)
as.data.frame(ilm_average(p_cells, weights = "count"))
```

Half the weight is on the youngest cell, so the average sits below the
middle cell's prediction.

## How uncertain

A prediction carries the fit's uncertainty by drawing the parameters. The
`uncertainty` argument says how much is drawn:

* `"joint"` (the default): every parameter, the variances included;
* `"fixed"`: the variances held at their estimates, everything else drawn;
* `"latent"`: every parameter held, and only the random effects drawn;
* `"none"`: the plug-in prediction at the estimates.

With 30 clinics the four choices give nearly the same interval for a new
clinic (not shown). With few clinics they don't, so the rest of this vignette uses 8. The model is fitted by maximum likelihood
(`reml = FALSE`), to be compared with restricted maximum likelihood below.

```{r few}
clinics8 <- simulate_clinics(8, seed = 2026)
fit8 <- illume::ilm_model(visits ~ I(age - 50) + (1 | clinic), data = clinics8,
                          family = "poisson", reml = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
```

The 90% interval for a new clinic's mean, under each choice:

```{r uncertainty}
widths <- sapply(c("joint", "fixed", "latent", "none"), function(u) {
  p <- suppressWarnings(ilm_predict(fit8, new_clinic, groups = "new", uncertainty = u, nsim = 2000))
  a <- as.data.frame(p)
  c(lower = a$lower_0.9, upper = a$upper_0.9, width = a$upper_0.9 - a$lower_0.9)
})
round(widths, 2)
```

Here the more that is drawn, the wider the interval. For a new clinic,
`"latent"` and `"none"` agree: both hold the parameters, and the new clinic's
effect is drawn either way. In limn's prototype study of few groups
(`studies/prototypes/`), `"joint"` came closest to nominal coverage for a new
unit's observation, though still below it: 0.88 for 90% intervals with 8
groups, against 0.85 to 0.87 for the other methods it tried, each with a
simulation standard error of about 0.01. (`suppressWarnings()`
hides a warning here, the few-groups check for means; the next section turns
to the few-groups checks.)

## The few-groups check, and its remedy

With so few clinics, the variance between them is poorly determined, and
intervals for a new clinic cover less often than they say. `ilm_predict()`
warns, says why, and names the remedy:

```{r warn-ml}
p8 <- ilm_predict(fit8, new_clinic, target = "response", groups = "new", nsim = 1000)
```

Maas and Hox (2005, pp. 86 and 89-90) found the standard errors of the
variances between groups too small with 50 groups or fewer, in linear
multilevel models. The remedy the warning names is to refit by restricted
maximum likelihood:

```{r warn-reml}
fit8_reml <- illume::ilm_model(visits ~ I(age - 50) + (1 | clinic), data = clinics8,
                               family = "poisson", reml = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
p8_reml <- ilm_predict(fit8_reml, new_clinic, target = "response", groups = "new", nsim = 1000)
```

The check still warns, since 8 clinics are still few, but it no longer offers
the refit: the fit already used it. It says what limn's study found with it,
and that more groups is the sure cure.

For a mean rather than a new observation, a related check warns that the
intervals are somewhat too narrow, and that no remedy for them has been
measured yet; see the Checks section of `?ilm_predict`. With the 30 clinics
above, neither check warns.

## Reading a prediction

`as.data.frame()` gives each row's estimate, mean and 90% interval;
`summary()` gives the 50% and 90% intervals. Their `new_level` column is
`TRUE` only for a row naming a clinic the fit has not seen, predicted under
`groups = "fitted"` as a new one.

```{r summary}
summary(ilm_predict(fit, new_clinic, groups = "new", nsim = 1000))
```

Maas, C. J. M. and Hox, J. J. (2005). Sufficient sample sizes for multilevel
modeling. *Methodology* 1(3), 86-92. Pp. 86 and 89-90.
